prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, enabling measurement of time and frequency at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a clean case of the discovery-or-invention criterion that I invoke when I describe how the committee works. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removed the lattice light shift, which was the obstacle to using many neutral atoms at once. Ye's group then turned that idea into the accuracy and stability frontier, with fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. The result is lasting and demonstrated in many laboratories, and it already supports tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and the planned redefinition of the second. Six of eight members place it in their top three, and the support comes from members whose own fields differ widely. That breadth persuades me more than the first-place count does. The credit also fits two people cleanly, so the prize avoids the three-person squeeze that burdens most other entries.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty margin. Frequency combs (Hall and Hansch, 2005) and ion-trap control (Wineland, 2012) have already been honoured, so a lattice-clock prize can look like a continuation of a single precision-timekeeping story rather than a new discovery. The scientific payoff, such as a redefinition of the second or a detected variation of constants, is still partly prospective. Other lattice-clock groups and the ion-clock line (Al+ and others) are not credited, so the boundary around Katori and Ye is defensible but not unique. I also rank my own first choice, B021, below this because I want to weigh my field against a neutral standard.

responses.point: The optical lattice clock combines Katori's magic-wavelength proposal with Ye's clocks at 1e-18 uncertainty, and the two decisive contributions fit a two-person prize, though ion clocks form a parallel line that might need joint recognition.
responses.response: I agree on attribution, and I would not widen the prize to ion clocks. Wineland was honoured in 2012 for control of single quantum systems, and joining a second technology would dilute a prize whose invention is crisp. The remaining weakness I share is that the strongest consequences, redefinition of the second and geodesy, are not yet realised. I would judge the prize on what has been demonstrated, which is orders-of-magnitude gains in systematic control and independent confirmation across laboratories.

responses.point: Lattice clocks offer a clear instrument advance beyond the caesium standard, with two natural laureates, while the choice between pairing with other clock technologies and waiting for the redefinition of the second is open.
responses.response: I respect the precision-measurement argument but I disagree with waiting for the formal redefinition. A prize should recognise the invention and its demonstrated performance, not an administrative decision by metrology bodies that the physics has already motivated. I also differ from your second choice, B010: the 2012 prize on controlling single quantum systems overlaps with the trapped-ion line, and the credit there (Cirac, Zoller, Blatt) is harder to separate cleanly.

responses.point: Circuit QED made the superconducting qubit a controllable system and is an enormous field, but the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits may make another superconducting-circuit award feel too close in time.
responses.response: I take the timing point seriously and it is the main reason I do not put B051 above B012. Where I qualify your view is that your own proximity to this field makes your top rank harder for me to discount, and I note the same about my own B021. Your second choice, B012, is where our views converge, and I would rather build on that overlap than defend a first place that relies on the field I know best.

responses.point: Twisted bilayer graphene joins band-structure theory with a tunable many-body platform and opened a large field, with a clean theory-plus-experiment split in the credited trio.
responses.response: I ranked B036 second myself and I accept the originality and speed of the field. My qualification is maturity: the pairing mechanism and the origin of the correlated states are unresolved, and a citation would have to describe the observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity without implying understanding. The Cao and Dean experimental contributions are also uncomfortable to leave out. I keep it as my first alternative, not my preferred choice, and I would revisit it as the mechanism clarifies.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the novelty margin over frequency combs and ion clocks as sufficient for a separate prize.
How much weight to give prospective impacts, such as the redefinition of the second and clock-based geodesy, versus demonstrated results.
Whether other lattice-clock groups, for example in Paris and elsewhere, require a different allocation of credit; I rely on general knowledge here and have not verified roles.
statement.conflict_note: Göran Johansson is also at Chalmers, so any Chalmers-linked candidate would need a concrete check; none of the shortlisted names is specifically tied to Chalmers in my profile. My own first choice, B021 (aberration-corrected electron optics), is in my field of transmission electron microscopy, and I have documented connections to the microscopy community through the International Federation of Societies for Microscopy. I would step back from deciding on B021 if it were advanced. For B012, no specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile.
